```markdown
<!-- .claude/skills/changelog-draft/SKILL.md -->
---
allowed-tools: Bash(git:*) Read
argument-hint: <tag>
description: Use when writing release notes for a tag.
disable-model-invocation: true
license: MIT
metadata:
    owner: docs-team
    tags:
        - docs
        - release
name: changelog-draft
paths:
    - CHANGELOG.md
# Content-Hash: blake3:9aae4dd1...
---

# Changelog draft

1. Run `scripts/changes.sh <tag>` to list the merged pull requests.
2. Group them under Features, Fixes and Chores.


## Resources

This skill bundles supporting files. Read them on demand when the task calls for them — don't bulk-load.

### Scripts

- `scripts/changes.sh`
```

The shared tree gets the portable keys only, so `argument-hint` is left out:

```markdown
<!-- .agents/skills/changelog-draft/SKILL.md -->
---
name: changelog-draft
description: "Use when writing release notes for a tag."
allowed-tools: Bash(git:*) Read
disable-model-invocation: true
license: MIT
metadata:
  owner: docs-team
  tags:
    - docs
    - release
paths:
  - CHANGELOG.md
# Content-Hash: blake3:9aae4dd1...
---
...
```

#### Frontmatter keys

| Key                        | Type    | Meaning                                                                                       |
| -------------------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                     | string  | The skill name. Defaults to the directory name.                                               |
| `description`              | string  | What the skill does and when to use it. Tools list it to decide when to load the skill.       |
| `license`                  | string  | [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/specification) field.                                   |
| `compatibility`            | string  | Agent Skills field: environment requirements (`Needs git and gh`).                            |
| `metadata`                 | map     | Agent Skills field: free-form keys. The spec expects string values; nested values are passed through as written. |
| `allowed-tools`            | string  | Agent Skills field: space-separated tools the skill may use.                                  |
| `paths` (or `globs`)       | list    | Load the skill only when matching files are in play; see [Path-gated skills](#path-gated-skills). |
| `disable-model-invocation` | boolean | `true`: only the user can invoke the skill; see [Invocation keys](#invocation-keys).          |
| `user-invocable`           | boolean | `false`: hide the skill from the `/` menu.                                                    |
| `delivery`                 | string  | `static`, `served` or `both`; see [Dynamic loading](#dynamic-loading-delivery). Never written to output. |
| `priority`, `targets`      |         | As for [rules](rules.md#frontmatter): ordering and the outputs the skill is written to.       |
| any other key              |         | Passed through to Claude Code (`model`, `context`, `hooks`, `argument-hint`, ...).            |

Output frontmatter is deterministic: collections are written in block style, aliases are resolved and comments are
dropped. In `.claude/skills/` all keys are sorted; in the other skill trees `name` and `description` come first and
the rest are sorted.

#### What each preset writes

| Key                                                     | Claude Code (`.claude/skills/`) | Every other skill tree (`.agents/skills/`, `.github/skills/`, ...) |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `name`, `description`                                   | yes                             | yes                                                                |
| `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`, `allowed-tools` | yes                             | yes                                                                |
| `paths`                                                 | yes                             | yes (read by Cursor; ignored by tools without a skill path gate)   |
| `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`            | yes                             | yes                                                                |
| `delivery`                                              | no                              | no                                                                 |
| any other key                                           | yes                             | no                                                                 |

Other tools get only the keys above because some consumers reject unknown keys (Claude.ai uploads and the Skills API
accept only the Agent Skills fields). The [`generate --plugin`](plugins.md) bundle copies `SKILL.md` as written.

#### Invocation keys

`user-invocable` and `disable-model-invocation` are yours: ai-rulez never overwrites a value you set. Use a YAML
boolean; another value (`"no"`, `"off"`) is reported as `AR304`.

- By default a skill is user-invocable, the key is not written, and the skill appears in the `/` menu.
- `[claude.skills] hide_from_menu = true` writes `user-invocable: false` into every Claude Code skill that does not
  set the key. A skill with its own `user-invocable: true` stays visible.
- Commands rendered as skills keep `user-invocable: true` unless the command sets the key.
- Codex has no `SKILL.md` key for this. When the `codex` preset writes its own skill tree (`agents_md = false`),
  `disable-model-invocation: true` adds `agents/openai.yaml` with `policy: { allow_implicit_invocation: false }`, so
  Codex runs the skill only when you name it with `$changelog-draft`.

```toml
[claude.skills]
hide_from_menu = true
```

#### Path-gated skills

`paths` (or `globs`) makes Claude Code and Cursor load a skill only when files matching the globs are in play. The
syntax is the same as for rule [`paths`](rules.md#frontmatter). Tools without a skill path gate ignore the key and
list the skill as usual.

#### Hooks that run bundled scripts

A skill's `hooks` key (Claude Code) runs commands while the skill is active. Claude Code sets `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` to
the skill's own directory, so a hook can reach a bundled script from any working directory:

```yaml
hooks:
  PostToolUse:
    - matcher: Edit
      hooks:
        - type: command
          command: "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/check.sh"
```

`validate` resolves the path against the skill directory: a missing file is `AR501`, and a script run
directly (not through `bash` or another interpreter) without the executable bit is `AR502`. The variable is defined
only for skills, not for agent or command hooks.

#### Dynamic loading (`delivery`)

`delivery` decides how a skill reaches the agent:

| Value              | Effect                                                                                     |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `static` (default) | written into every tool's skill folder                                                     |
| `served`           | left out of the skill folders and served on demand by `ai-rulez mcp --serve-skills`        |
| `both`             | written to the folders and served                                                          |

```yaml
# .ai-rulez/skills/db-migrations/SKILL.md, under x-ai-rulez.metadata
delivery: served
triggers: [schema change, alembic migration, add a column]
```

When any skill is served, each tool's skill folder gets a `dynamic-skills` skill that tells the agent to call
`find_skill` and `load_skill`, and the default `ai-rulez` MCP server entry starts with `--serve-skills`.

The default comes from, in order: the skill's own `delivery`, the [role's](roles.md#delivery) `delivery`,
`[domains.<name>] delivery`, `[skills] delivery`, then `static`. A project can serve a whole domain, or every skill,
and mark a few core skills `static`:

```toml
[skills]
delivery = "served"
```

Warnings to know:

| Code    | When                                                                                                         |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `AR992` | A served skill targets a tool that cannot call MCP tools; it is written there as a static file.             |
| `AR993` | Skills are served but no MCP server entry runs `ai-rulez mcp --serve-skills`.                               |
| `AR9R0` | A `served` skill runs a bundled `scripts/` or `assets/` file by relative path. Nothing is on disk to run; use `delivery: both`. |
| `AR9R1` | Always-loaded content points at a `both` skill with `disable-model-invocation: true` by name; the model's Skill tool refuses it. Point at the file path instead. |
| `AR9R2` | A `served` skill sets `disable-model-invocation: true`: it is written nowhere and hidden from the model, so nobody can run it. |

An MCP client that must keep a skill served can still fetch its files with `list_skill_resources` and
`read_skill_file`; see [Dynamic skill loading](mcp-server.md#dynamic-skill-loading).

#### Size limits

`generate` and `tokens` warn when a root instruction file exceeds a limit the tool documents. See
[Rules: size limits](rules.md#size-limits).

#### See also

- [Installed skills](installed-skills.md): skills fetched from other repositories.
- [AGENTS.md and .agents/skills](agents-md.md): the shared skill tree.

## Checks

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/checks/

A check is a code-review guideline: one topic a review tool (Cursor Bugbot, Kilo Code Reviews, GitLab Duo, Augment,
Amp, ...) applies to every pull or merge request. You write each check once in `.ai-rulez/checks/`, and `generate`
writes it into the review file each enabled tool reads.

#### Example

```bash
ai-rulez add check security --severity high --description "Flags common security issues"
```

```markdown
<!-- .ai-rulez/checks/security.md -->
---
type: Reference
title: Security
description: Flags common security issues
x-ai-rulez:
  kind: check
  id: security
  metadata:
    severity: high
---

Review the diff for injection vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets and unsafe
deserialization. Report each finding with a file and line reference.
```

```toml
# .ai-rulez/config.toml
presets = ["cursor", "kilo", "amp", "augment"]
```

After `ai-rulez generate`, Cursor Bugbot and Kilo get a section in a shared markdown file. If `REVIEW.md` already
holds your own text, the block is appended below it:

```markdown
<!-- REVIEW.md -->
This repository has no review notes yet.

<!-- ai-rulez:checks:begin -->
<!-- ai-rulez:check:security -->

## security

Review the diff for injection vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets and unsafe
deserialization. Report each finding with a file and line reference.
<!-- ai-rulez:checks:end -->
```

Amp gets one file per check, with its metadata in the frontmatter (`tools` too, when the check sets them):

```markdown
<!-- .agents/checks/security.md -->
---
description: Flags common security issues
name: security
severity-default: high
---

Review the diff for injection vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets and unsafe
deserialization. Report each finding with a file and line reference.
```

Augment gets an area in its YAML file:

```yaml
# .augment/code_review_guidelines.yaml
areas:
  security:
    description: Flags common security issues
    globs:
      - '**'
    rules:
      - description: |-
          Review the diff for injection vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets and unsafe
          deserialization. Report each finding with a file and line reference.
        id: security
        severity: high
```

#### Source files

```text
.ai-rulez/checks/<name>.md
.ai-rulez/domains/<domain>/checks/<name>.md
.ai-rulez/local/checks/<name>.md        machine-local, gitignored
```

The file name is the check's identity. It may contain only letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, since it becomes part
of output paths and section markers; `validate` rejects anything else. As for [rules](rules.md#rule-files), `type` is
required in a tree created by `init`; create checks with `ai-rulez add check`, or run `ai-rulez generate` after
writing one by hand so the `index.md` listings include it. Two names that differ only in case count as
one check, and the higher-precedence source wins.

Root checks are always included; domain checks are included when the domain is in the active
[profile](domains.md) or [role](roles.md). A root check shadows a domain check of the same name.

| Key           | Type   | Default      | Meaning                                                                         |
| ------------- | ------ | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `description` | string | none         | Short summary. Used as the text when the body is empty.                         |
| `severity`    | string | none         | `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical`. Any other value fails validation.        |
| `tools`       | list   | none         | Tools the check may use. Only Amp has a place for them.                         |
| `targets`     | list   | every preset | Presets, paths or globs the check is written to, as for [rules](rules.md#targets). `add check` and `update_check` reject a misspelt preset name. |

#### Managing checks

```bash
ai-rulez add check security --description "Security issues" --severity high
ai-rulez add check sql-injection --domain backend --targets "src/**/*.go"
ai-rulez list checks [--domain backend] [--format json]
ai-rulez remove check security [--domain backend] [--yes]
```

The [MCP server](mcp-server.md) has `create_check`, `read_check`, `update_check`, `delete_check` and `list_checks`.
`update_check` takes new `content`, fields (`description`, `severity`, `tools`, `targets`), or both. Content without
frontmatter replaces only the body and keeps the existing frontmatter.

An [include](includes.md) can import checks with `include = ["checks"]`.

#### Where they are written

| Preset       | Output                                       | Shape                                                       |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cursor`     | `.cursor/BUGBOT.md`                          | one block, one section per check (Bugbot)                   |
| `kilo`       | `REVIEW.md`                                  | one block, one section per check                            |
| `qwen`       | `.qwen/review-rules.md`                      | one block, one section per check                            |
| `rovodev`    | `.rovodev/.review-agent.md`                  | one block, one section per check                            |
| `factory`    | `.factory/skills/review-guidelines/SKILL.md` | one block in a skill with `name` and `description` frontmatter |
| `amp`        | `.agents/checks/<name>.md`                   | one file per check                                          |
| `augment`    | `.augment/code_review_guidelines.yaml`       | one area per check, merged into your YAML                   |
| `gitlab-duo` | `.gitlab/duo/mr-review-instructions.yaml`    | one `instructions` group per check, merged into your YAML   |

##### Shared markdown files

ai-rulez owns only the block between `<!-- ai-rulez:checks:begin -->` and `<!-- ai-rulez:checks:end -->`. Each check
in it is a `<!-- ai-rulez:check:<name> -->` marker, a `## <name>` heading and the check text:

```md
<!-- ai-rulez:checks:begin -->
<!-- ai-rulez:check:security -->

## security

Review the diff for injection vulnerabilities...
<!-- ai-rulez:checks:end -->
```

- Text outside the block is yours and survives every `generate`. An existing file gets the block appended.
- `clean`, or removing the last check, removes only the block. A file that held nothing else is deleted; a file with
  your text is never deleted or gitignored.
- Do not edit inside the block (the next `generate` rewrites it) and do not put the marker lines in a check's text.
  `generate` fails rather than touch a file whose markers do not pair up.
- Severity and tools have no equivalent in these files and are not written.
- For `factory`, the skill frontmatter is written once, when the file is created. A skill of your own named
  `review-guidelines` collides with it, and `generate` fails until one is renamed.

##### Augment and GitLab Duo YAML

Both files are documented as hand-written, so ai-rulez merges into them. It owns only the areas (Augment) or groups
(GitLab Duo) named after its checks, keeps everything else (`file_paths_to_ignore`, your own entries, comments and key
order), and removes its entries when a check is deleted.

- An entry you wrote under a check's name is yours: it is never replaced, the check is not written there, and
  `generate` warns. Rename one of them.
- An entry ai-rulez wrote becomes yours once you edit it.
- Augment's severity scale stops at `high`: `critical` is written as `high`, and an unset severity as `medium`. Every
  area gets `globs: ["**"]`.
- GitLab Duo groups have `name` and `instructions` only, with no file filter.

#### Tool notes

- **Commit the outputs.** A hosted reviewer reads only committed files, usually from the base branch of the pull
  request. Check outputs are never added to the managed `.gitignore` block, even with `gitignore = true`.
- **Kilo** reads `REVIEW.md` only when **Use REVIEW.md** is enabled in the Kilo web app, and truncates it at 10,000
  characters. `generate` warns when the file, your text included, is longer.
- **Bugbot** also reads nested `<dir>/.cursor/BUGBOT.md` files, which ai-rulez does not generate. `generate --user`
  writes no Bugbot file.
- **Amp**: the format follows the rulesync documentation, since Amp's own manual does not describe it. Verify it
  against your Amp version.
- **Local checks** (`.ai-rulez/local/checks/`) are written only for presets with one file per check (Amp), as a
  gitignored file. Shared files never take a local check, and a warning names the presets that skipped it. A local
  check may not share a name with a shared one.
- `ai-rulez doctor` and `ai-rulez tokens` include the check files.

Not generated: Augment per-area globs, GitLab `fileFilters`, Takt quality gates, Hermes pre-verify specs, and
JetBrains AI Assistant (its self-review path is a per-user IDE setting).

## OKF (Open Knowledge Format)

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/okf/

[OKF](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format/blob/main/SPEC.md) is a directory of markdown files
with YAML frontmatter, meant to be read by people and by agents. ai-rulez implements OKF spec 0.2. You can:

- export your rules, context, skills, agents, commands and checks as an OKF bundle, and keep it in sync with the `okf`
  preset;
- import an OKF bundle into `.ai-rulez/`, or use one directly as an [include](#okf-bundles-as-includes);
- lint any bundle with `ai-rulez okf validate`;
- store `.ai-rulez/` itself as an OKF bundle (the [native tree](#the-native-tree), which `init` creates).

#### Example

```bash
ai-rulez export okf
```

```text
Wrote 4 files to /home/dev/acme/docs/okf (2 rules)
```

```text
docs/okf/
├── .okf-export.json
├── index.md
└── rules/
    ├── commit-messages.md
    ├── index.md
    └── typescript.md
```

```markdown
<!-- docs/okf/index.md -->
---
okf_version: "0.2"
---

# Subdirectories

- [rules](rules/index.md) - Rules exported from ai-rulez
```

```markdown
<!-- docs/okf/rules/typescript.md -->
---
type: Decision
title: Typescript
x-ai-rulez:
  kind: rule
  id: typescript
  metadata:
    paths:
      - src/**/*.{ts,tsx}
---

Prefer `type` over `interface` for unions. No `any`.
```

Any OKF reader sees a `Decision` concept titled "Typescript". ai-rulez reads the `x-ai-rulez` key back, so
`export okf`, `import okf`, `export okf` is byte-identical.

Importing a bundle someone else wrote:

```bash
ai-rulez okf validate ../kb
ai-rulez import okf ../kb --dry-run
```

```text
would create     .ai-rulez/context/tables-orders.md
would create     .ai-rulez/skills/runbooks-deploy/SKILL.md
index style: body
Summary: 2 created, 0 overwritten, 0 unchanged, 0 conflicts, 0 skipped
```

A `BigQuery Table` concept at `tables/orders.md` became context, and a `Playbook` at `runbooks/deploy.md` became a
skill. See [Import mapping](#import-mapping).

#### Mapping

Each ai-rulez item becomes one OKF concept. The `type` is for OKF readers; the identity lives in the `x-ai-rulez`
extension key.

| ai-rulez                  | OKF `type` written | Notes                                                                    |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| rule                      | `Decision`         |                                                                          |
| context                   | `Concept`          |                                                                          |
| skill                     | `Playbook`         | `SKILL.md`; `references/`, `scripts/` and `assets/` next to it          |
| agent, command, check     | `Reference`        | OKF has no such types; `x-ai-rulez.kind` restores them                  |
| skill resource (markdown) | `Reference`        | wrapped in frontmatter so the bundle stays conformant; unwrapped on import |

Set `type` (or `title`) in an item's `okf` frontmatter map to write a different value, for example
`okf: {type: Policy}` on a rule.

Frontmatter of every exported concept:

```yaml
---
type: Decision
title: Testing                 # the id in words, unless okf.title is set
description: One line          # the item's description, when it has one
x-ai-rulez:
  kind: rule                   # rule | context | skill | agent | command | check | skill-resource
  id: testing
  domain: backend              # only for domain content
  metadata:                    # every other frontmatter key, with its YAML type
    priority: high
    globs: ["**/*_test.go"]
---
```

Layout of an exported bundle:

```text
index.md                              okf_version, then one entry per kind directory
rules/index.md  rules/<id>.md
context/<id>.md
skills/<id>/SKILL.md                  + index.md, references/, scripts/, assets/
agents/<id>.md  commands/<id>.md  checks/<id>.md
domains/<domain>/<kind>/...           same shape for domain content
```

- Every directory with a concept gets an `index.md`, entries sorted by path, each with the concept's description.
- No `log.md`, timestamps or `generated` fields are written, so the output is deterministic; history is git's.
- Bodies are copied byte for byte. Executable bits of scripts are kept.
- A name that is not safe in a path is written to a transliterated path and restored from `x-ai-rulez.id` on import.
  An item named `index` or `log` is stored as `index_.md` / `log_.md`, since OKF reserves those names.

##### Import mapping

A concept with `x-ai-rulez.kind` is imported as that kind. Otherwise its `type` decides (case-insensitive, `-`, `_`
and spaces ignored):

| OKF type                                                            | Becomes |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `decision`, `rule`, `convention`, `policy`, `guideline`, `standard` | rule    |
| `howto`, `playbook`, `runbook`, `procedure`, `skill`                | skill   |
| anything else (`concept`, `reference`, `metric`, `BigQuery Table`, ...) | context |

- The item id is the concept's path with `/` turned into `-` (`runbooks/deploy.md` becomes the skill
  `runbooks-deploy`). Rename and refine afterwards: a skill needs a description that says when to use it.
- `--into rules|context|skills` forces every concept to one kind; `--domain <name>` places everything in a domain.
- OKF keys with no ai-rulez equivalent (`tags`, `resource`, `sources`, `status`, `stale_after`, a foreign `type` or
  `title`, ...) are kept in an `okf` frontmatter map, and `export okf` writes them back at the top level:

  ```yaml
  ---
  description: The orders table
  okf:
    type: BigQuery Table
    title: Orders
    tags: [sales]
  ---
  ```

- Links between imported concepts are rewritten to the relative path of the created file
  (`/runbooks/deploy.md` becomes `../skills/runbooks-deploy/SKILL.md`). A link to a file that was not imported is
  left as written and reported as `AR9B9`. On export, relative links between exported items become bundle-absolute
  (`/context/architecture.md`). Links in code blocks are never touched.
- Non-markdown files are imported only from `references/`, `scripts/` or `assets/` next to a skill. `log.md` and
  `index.md` are not imported.
- `import okf` writes the files with their keys at the top level. In a [native tree](#the-native-tree), run
  `ai-rulez migrate okf` afterwards so `validate` sees the OKF shape.

##### Import report

`import okf --format json` prints:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "source": "../kb",
  "target": ".ai-rulez",
  "dry_run": false,
  "index_style": "body",
  "actions": [
    { "path": "context/tables-orders.md", "kind": "context", "status": "created", "source": "tables/orders.md" },
    { "path": "skills/runbooks-deploy/SKILL.md", "kind": "skills", "status": "created", "source": "runbooks/deploy.md" }
  ],
  "findings": [],
  "security": [],
  "skipped": []
}
```

| Field         | Meaning                                                                                     |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `actions`     | one entry per file: `path` (relative to `target`), `kind`, `status` and the bundle `source` |
| `status`      | `created`, `overwritten`, `unchanged` or `conflict` (the file exists and differs)           |
| `findings`    | `AR9B*` findings for the bundle, with `code`, `name`, `severity`, `path`, `line`, `message` |
| `security`    | `AR001`-`AR011` findings; any error refuses the whole import                                |
| `skipped`     | files not imported (symlinks, unsupported files)                                            |

Exit codes: `0` done; `2` refused by the security scan, or files exist and differ (rerun with `--force` to
overwrite); `1` the bundle could not be read.

##### Titles and conflicts

`title` is the item id in words (`code-style` is "Code Style") unless the item has `okf.title`. An import keeps a
bundle title that differs as `okf.title`, so an edited title survives export, edit, `import --force`, export.

- `import okf` never overwrites a file that differs unless you pass `--force`; then the bundle wins.
- `export okf` and `generate` write the sources' title, so a title edited only in the bundle is drift (`AR9B5`).
  Run `generate` to restore the source, or `import okf --force` to adopt the edit.

##### Index styles

Two `index.md` schemes are in use. ai-rulez reads both and writes the one you configure; concept files are identical
in both.

| Style              | `index_style`   | Shape                                                                                  |
| ------------------ | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Body (default)     | `"body"`        | OKF 0.2: no frontmatter except `okf_version` at the root; `# Concepts` and `# Subdirectories` headings with `- [Title](file.md) - description` bullets |
| Frontmatter        | `"frontmatter"` | `title`, `version: 0.1.0` and an `entries` list in the frontmatter, no body (the scheme described on the [OKF website](https://okf.md/)); the root also keeps `okf_version` |

```yaml
---
okf_version: "0.2"
title: Index
version: 0.1.0
entries:
  - title: rules
    path: rules/index.md
    description: Rules exported from ai-rulez
---
```

Set it with `[okf] index_style` or `export okf --index-style` (the flag wins). `generate --check` and
`export okf --check` compare the configured style, so a bundle in the other style is drift.

#### The native tree

`ai-rulez init` creates `.ai-rulez/` as an OKF bundle, and `ai-rulez migrate okf` converts an older tree in place:
the frontmatter of every item moves under `x-ai-rulez.metadata`, `type` and `title` are added, and each directory gets
an `index.md` (the root one names `okf_version`). The generated output does not change.

```bash
ai-rulez migrate okf --dry-run   # list what would change
ai-rulez migrate okf             # convert; running it again changes nothing
ai-rulez migrate okf --check     # exit 2 while files still need migrating
```

- `type`, `title` and `x-ai-rulez` are reserved keys. The loader reads `x-ai-rulez.metadata` (and any other
  top-level key) as the item's frontmatter.
- Only `type` is required (without it, `AR9B1`). `title`, `description` and `x-ai-rulez` are optional:
  `x-ai-rulez.kind` defaults to the directory and `x-ai-rulez.id` to the file or skill directory name. `add` and
  `init` write all of them.
- `add`, `remove` and the MCP CRUD tools write this form and refresh the `index.md` files. Once the root `index.md`
  lists its directories, `generate` refreshes stale indexes too, including after you add files by hand. For files
  without OKF keys, `migrate okf` adds them and rewrites the indexes in one step.
- `validate` runs the OKF checks (`AR9B*`) on such a tree, together with every other analyzer; `--analyzer okf` runs
  them alone.
- A tree without a root `index.md` uses the older layout. It still loads, with a deprecation notice from `validate`,
  `generate` and `list`. See [Migrating to v5](migration-v5.md#okf-is-the-format-of-ai-rulez).

What `migrate okf` does not do:

- **Reserved names.** If an item is named `index` or `log` (`rules/index.md`), the migration refuses before writing
  anything, names the files and exits 1. Rename them and run it again.
- **Symlinks** are never followed or rewritten. They are listed as `[skipped]`, and the run exits 1; replace the link
  with the real file. A file whose frontmatter does not parse is skipped the same way.
- **Backups.** Before rewriting, the originals are copied to `<config dir>.bak-okf-<timestamp>/`. `validate` ignores
  that directory; delete it once you have reviewed the result.

#### Codes

`AR9B0`-`AR9B9` are the OKF codes, reported by `okf validate`, `validate` and `doctor`. See
[Strict validation](strict-validation.md).

| Code    | Name                     | Default | Finds                                                                                             |
| ------- | ------------------------ | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AR9B0` | `okf-index-mismatch`     | warning | an index entry that points at a missing file, a concept or subdirectory the index does not list, or an index whose titles or descriptions are stale |
| `AR9B1` | `okf-type-invalid`       | error   | unparseable frontmatter, a missing or empty `type`, or an unknown `x-ai-rulez.kind`; a `kind` that disagrees with its directory is a warning |
| `AR9B2` | `okf-link-broken`        | warning | a relative or bundle-relative link whose target is not in the bundle                              |
| `AR9B3` | `okf-version-invalid`    | warning | a root `okf_version` that is not `MAJOR.MINOR` (info when it is not `0.2`, or for a frontmatter-style root index you did not configure); an error from `okf validate` when there is no root `index.md` with `okf_version` |
| `AR9B4` | `okf-orphan`             | info    | a concept no index entry or link reaches (only when the bundle has an index)                     |
| `AR9B5` | `okf-export-drift`       | error   | the configured bundle differs from what `export okf` would write now                              |
| `AR9B6` | `okf-reserved-structure` | error   | frontmatter keys an `index.md` may not have; a `log.md` heading that is not an ISO date (warning) |
| `AR9B7` | `okf-title-duplicate`    | info    | two concepts in one directory with the same title                                                 |
| `AR9B8` | `okf-path-unsafe`        | error   | a symlink, a path escaping the bundle, a file over the size limit, or two paths that differ only in case |
| `AR9B9` | `okf-lossy-mapping`      | info    | from `import okf`: `x-ai-rulez` data that cannot be mapped, or a link to a file that was not imported |

Unknown `type` values, unknown keys and missing optional fields are allowed by the spec and never reported.

#### Commands

| Command                                                                       | Does                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`export okf`](cli-reference.md#ai-rulez-export-okf) `[--output-dir dir] [--profile p \| --role r] [--include kinds] [--index-style s] [--check]` | write, or with `--check` compare, the bundle |
| [`import okf`](cli-reference.md#ai-rulez-import-okf) `<dir\|git-url> [--into kind] [--domain d] [--dry-run] [--force]` | bundle to `.ai-rulez/` sources |
| [`migrate okf`](cli-reference.md#ai-rulez-migrate-okf) `[--dry-run] [--check]` | convert `.ai-rulez/` in place to an OKF bundle            |
| [`okf validate`](cli-reference.md#ai-rulez-okf-validate) `<dir\|git-url> [--fail-on sev] [--format json]` | lint any bundle; exit 2 on findings at `--fail-on` (default `error`) |
| [`convert --from okf`](cli-reference.md#ai-rulez-convert)                     | the import mapping through convert's plan, lossiness report and `--merge`; finds a bundle at the source root or in `docs/okf` |

- `export okf --role r` exports the slice of content a [role](roles.md) selects, like `generate --role`. Served skills
  are exported like static ones; `skill_mode` is not exported.
- `export okf` records the files it wrote in `.okf-export.json` and only ever removes files listed there, so files
  you add to the bundle directory are never pruned. It refuses an `--output-dir` that is, contains or lies inside the
  configuration directory.
- A remote source is `https://host/org/repo[.git][@ref][#subdir]`, `git@host:org/repo[@ref]` or
  `file:///path/repo[@ref]`. Plain `http://` is refused. Git runs without hooks, prompts or submodules.

#### Configuration

```toml
presets = ["claude", "cursor", "okf"]   # the okf preset keeps the bundle in sync on generate

[okf]
dir = "docs/okf"                         # default
include = ["rules", "context", "skills"] # default: every kind
spec = "0.2"                             # the only accepted value
index_style = "body"                     # or "frontmatter"
```

| Key           | Type   | Default    | Meaning                                                      |
| ------------- | ------ | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `dir`         | string | `docs/okf` | where `export okf` and the preset write the bundle           |
| `include`     | list   | all kinds  | kinds to export: `rules`, `context`, `skills`, `agents`, `commands`, `checks` |
| `spec`        | string | `0.2`      | OKF version written                                          |
| `index_style` | string | `body`     | see [Index styles](#index-styles)                            |

The preset exports the profile `generate` runs with, from your own shared sources: never `.ai-rulez/local/`, and not
domains or items that come from builtins or includes. The bundle is committed documentation: `gitignore = true` never
ignores it, and it has no generated-by banner. `generate --check` and `doctor` report a hand-edited, missing or stale
bundle file as drift. While `generate --role` runs, the preset leaves the bundle untouched.

#### OKF bundles as includes

An OKF bundle can feed `generate` directly, without a one-time import:

```toml
[[includes]]
name = "team-kb"
source = "https://github.com/acme/knowledge"
ref = "v1.2"
path = "bundles/platform"     # directory of the bundle inside the source
format = "okf"
include = ["rules", "skills"]
```

The bundle is converted with the import mapping at load time and merged like any other [include](includes.md): same
precedence, same cache, same [lock file](lockfile.md) pinning, same `install_to`. The security scan runs on the
converted text, and a bundle with an error-level finding is refused as a whole.

#### Security

- Import never follows symlinks in a bundle (each is skipped with `AR9B8`) and writes only below the target
  directory. Ids and resource paths that are not plain names are rejected.
- All text, scripts included, is scanned with `AR001`-`AR011` before the first write; one error-level finding (a
  secret, hidden Unicode, `curl | sh`) refuses the whole import. `ignore` comments in imported text are not honored.
- Bundles are bounded (50,000 files, 8 MiB per file). Nothing in a bundle is executed.
- OKF content is instructions for agents: importing it from a stranger is like adding any other include. Read the
  `--dry-run` output first.

#### CI

```bash
ai-rulez generate --check                               # fails when docs/okf is stale (okf preset)
ai-rulez validate                                       # AR9B* for the configured bundle
ai-rulez okf validate docs/okf --fail-on warning --format json
```

Validate a third-party bundle before importing it:

```bash
ai-rulez okf validate https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format@main#bundles/acme_retail
ai-rulez import okf https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format@main#bundles/acme_retail \
  --domain acme --dry-run
```

#### Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                       | Cause and fix                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AR9B1` on a file you wrote by hand           | The file has no `type`. Add it, or run `ai-rulez migrate okf`.                                   |
| `AR9B0` / `AR9B4` after adding files by hand  | The `index.md` listings do not include them yet. Run `ai-rulez generate`.                       |
| A `.ai-rulez.bak-okf-*` directory appears     | A backup of rewritten files. Delete it after review, and do not commit it.                       |

#### Limitations

- Only OKF 0.2 is written. OKF 0.1 bundles (`timestamp`, `# Citations`) are read as they are.
- The trust, provenance and lifecycle fields (`sources`, `generated`, `verified`, `status`, `stale_after`) and the
  `Attested Computation` type are preserved but have no effect in ai-rulez.
- A foreign concept maps to exactly one kind.
- Agents, commands and checks travel as `Reference` with `x-ai-rulez.kind`. A tool that drops unknown keys loses
  that information.
- Key order and comments in a source file's frontmatter are normalized by an export.

## Domains and profiles

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/domains/

A **domain** is a named folder of content (`.ai-rulez/domains/<name>/`) for one team, service or area of the
project. A **profile** is a named list of domains. `generate --profile <name>` renders the root content plus the
domains the profile names, so the backend team's assistants get the backend rules and not the frontend ones.

#### Example

```text
.ai-rulez/
├── config.toml
├── rules/
│   └── commit-messages.md          root: every profile gets it
└── domains/
    ├── backend/
    │   └── rules/
    │       └── database.md
    └── frontend/
        └── rules/
            └── components.md       paths: ["web/**/*.tsx"]
```

```toml
# .ai-rulez/config.toml
presets = ["claude", "cursor", "gemini"]
default = "backend"

[profiles]
backend = ["backend"]
frontend = ["frontend"]
```

`ai-rulez init --domains backend,frontend` creates the folders, and `ai-rulez add rule` writes the rules:

```bash
ai-rulez add rule commit-messages --content "Use Conventional Commits."
ai-rulez add rule database --domain backend --priority critical \
  --content "Use prepared statements. Every schema change ships a migration."
```

```markdown
<!-- .ai-rulez/domains/backend/rules/database.md -->
---
type: Decision
title: Database
x-ai-rulez:
  kind: rule
  id: database
  domain: backend
  metadata:
    priority: critical
---

Use prepared statements. Every schema change ships a migration.
```

```markdown
<!-- .ai-rulez/domains/frontend/rules/components.md -->
---
type: Decision
title: Components
x-ai-rulez:
  kind: rule
  id: components
  domain: frontend
  metadata:
    paths: ["web/**/*.tsx"]
---

One component per file.
```

`add rule` writes `priority: medium` when you pass no `--priority`, which is why the root rule below shows a priority
line; a rule without an explicit `priority` has none.

`ai-rulez generate` uses the `default` profile, `backend`. The shared `AGENTS.md`, read by all three tools, holds the
root rule and the backend rule:

```markdown
<!-- AGENTS.md -->
...
# acme

## Rules

### database

**Priority:** critical

Use prepared statements. Every schema change ships a migration.

### commit-messages

**Priority:** medium

Use Conventional Commits.
```

`ai-rulez generate --profile frontend` replaces the backend rule with the frontend one. The scoped rule gets
`.claude/rules/components.md` and `.cursor/rules/components.mdc`; files of the previous profile are removed. Because
Gemini has no rules folder, `AGENTS.md` also inlines the scoped rule and `generate` warns; see
[Glob-scoped rules and AGENTS.md](rules.md#glob-scoped-rules-and-agentsmd).

#### Domain folders

A domain folder has the same layout as the root of `.ai-rulez/`:

```text
.ai-rulez/domains/<name>/
├── rules/
├── context/
├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
├── agents/
├── commands/
└── checks/
```

Any subset of these folders makes a domain. Domain names are folder names; use names that say who owns the content
(`backend`, `payments`, `mobile`), not `misc` or `shared`. Content everybody needs belongs at the root.

#### What a profile selects

A run renders:

- all root content;
- the domains the profile names;
- globally enabled [builtin](configuration.md) packs and every domain that comes from an [include](includes.md),
  whatever the profile.

Profiles also select [installed skills](installed-skills.md) and MCP servers that list them in their `profiles`
field.

| Setting                 | Meaning                                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `[profiles] <name> = [...]` | the domains the profile selects                                                            |
| `default`               | the profile `generate` uses without `--profile`                                               |
| `--profile <name>`      | select a profile for one run (`generate`, `tokens`, `export okf`, ...)                         |

With no profile selected and no `default` set, the built-in `default` profile applies: every domain when no
`[profiles]` are defined, otherwise only root content plus builtin and include-sourced domains. So once you add
`[profiles]` without a `default`, a plain `generate` drops all domain content and removes its outputs; `generate`
warns about this. Set a top-level `default = "<profile>"`, or define a profile named `default` (for example
`default = ["*"]` under `[profiles]`).

##### Domain list entries

| Entry            | Meaning                                                                                             |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"backend"`      | the domain `backend`                                                                                |
| `"*"`            | every domain the configuration knows                                                                |
| `"!frontend"`    | remove `frontend` from what the other entries selected                                              |
| `"builtin:docker"` | the builtin pack `docker`, for this profile only; `builtin:<name>/<item>` selects one item of a pack |

```toml
[profiles]
backend = ["backend", "builtin:docker"]
everything-but-mobile = ["*", "!mobile"]
```

- A list made only of `!` entries is an error: there is nothing to subtract from. Write `"*"` first.
- `builtin:<name>` works even when the root `builtins` setting is absent or `false`. A pack the root `builtins`
  setting enables stays global wherever else it is named.
- An unknown domain name selects nothing; loading the configuration logs a warning naming it.

#### Composing profiles

Select several profiles at once by separating their names with commas. The result is the union of their domains, in
the order they are first named:

```bash
ai-rulez generate --profile base,backend
ai-rulez tokens --profile base,backend
```

One profile can then hold what everybody installs, while the others add only their extras:

```toml
[profiles]
base = ["conventions", "security"]
backend = ["api", "database"]
frontend = ["web"]
```

`--profile base,backend` and `--profile base,frontend` cover both teams without a `base-backend` and `base-frontend`
profile each. A composed value works anywhere a profile name does, including `default` and a scope's `profile`:

```toml
default = "base,backend"
```

- Every element must be a defined profile. An unknown one is an error naming that element.
- Profile lists name domains, never other profiles, so composition is one level deep.
- The built-in `default` composes only if you defined a profile named `default`.
- Whitespace and empty elements are ignored: `base, backend` and `base,backend,` are the same.
- A profile name may not contain a comma.

#### Name collisions

When an item of the same kind and name exists in more than one place, one copy is kept and the others are dropped
with a warning naming both files:

```text
WARN  Duplicate rule collapsed name=database kept=.ai-rulez/rules/database.md dropped=.ai-rulez/domains/backend/rules/database.md
```

Precedence is root, then on-disk domain, then include-sourced domain, then builtin. It applies to rules, context,
skills, agents, commands and checks alike; see [Deduplication by name](configuration.md#deduplication-by-name). To
keep a rule specific to one domain, give it a name no other layer uses.

#### Domain settings

`[domains.<name>]` holds settings for one domain's content:

```toml
[domains.runbooks]
delivery = "served"    # serve this domain's skills over MCP instead of writing them
```

| Key        | Type   | Default  | Meaning                                                                         |
| ---------- | ------ | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `delivery` | string | `static` | default [delivery](skills.md#dynamic-loading-delivery) of the domain's skills   |

#### Profiles and roles

A profile answers "what does this repository ship". When the question is "what does a backend engineer, an on-call
responder or a support agent get on their machine", use [roles](roles.md): they add per-kind include and exclude
selectors, one level of inheritance and per-skill modes on top of a domain list, and are selected with
`generate --role`. See [Profiles vs roles](roles.md#profiles-vs-roles).

#### Moving to domains

To split a flat `.ai-rulez/rules/` into domains:

```bash
mkdir -p .ai-rulez/domains/backend/rules .ai-rulez/domains/frontend/rules
git mv .ai-rulez/rules/backend-api.md .ai-rulez/domains/backend/rules/api.md
git mv .ai-rulez/rules/frontend-components.md .ai-rulez/domains/frontend/rules/components.md
```

Then add the `[profiles]`, and check the result:

```bash
ai-rulez validate
ai-rulez generate --profile backend
```

In an [OKF tree](okf.md#the-native-tree), `generate` also refreshes the `index.md` listings of the folders you
changed.

#### Troubleshooting

| Symptom                              | Cause and fix                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Domain content is missing            | The domain is not in the active profile. Check `default` and `[profiles]`, or pass `--profile`.   |
| `profile not found: x`               | The name, or one element of a composed value, is not defined. The error lists the available ones.  |
| A domain rule never appears          | A root item with the same name wins. `validate` lists every collapsed duplicate.                  |
| Files of another profile remain      | They are removed by the next `generate`; hand-written files in rules folders are never touched.    |

## Roles

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/roles/

A role maps a job to the slice of the shared content a person needs: which domains, which skills, rules, agents,
commands and checks, and how each skill is surfaced. `generate --role <name>` renders that slice, for the project or
with `--user` for one person's machine. Use roles when one repository serves people with different jobs, such as
backend engineers, release managers and support agents.

!!! note "ai-rulez does not do identity"
    A role is a name. ai-rulez has no notion of users, groups or authentication. Something else (an identity-provider
    integration, a web UI, a wrapper script) decides who holds which role and runs `ai-rulez generate --role <name>`.
    The `match` hints on a role are strings for that tool; ai-rulez never interprets them.

#### Example

```toml
# .ai-rulez/config.toml
presets = ["claude", "cursor", "copilot"]

[role_manifest]
enabled = true                  # write .ai-rulez/roles.json on generate

[[roles]]
name = "engineer"
description = "Everyone who writes code"
domains = ["backend"]

[roles.skills]
exclude = ["deploy-*"]

[roles.skill_mode]
"review-*" = "name-only"

[roles.match]
groups = ["okta:eng"]

[[roles]]
name = "release-manager"
extends = "engineer"
domains = ["release"]

[roles.skill_mode]
deploy = "user-invocable-only"
```

The `backend` domain has the skills `review-pr` and `deploy-staging`; the `release` domain has `deploy`.

```bash
ai-rulez roles resolve release-manager
```

```text
role release-manager: 4 item(s), 895 bytes, ~237 tokens (cl100k_base)
KIND   DOMAIN   ID               MODE                 DELIVERY  BYTES  TOKENS
rule   -        commit-messages  -                    -         153    42
rule   backend  database         -                    -         156    43
skill  backend  review-pr        name-only            static    289    78
skill  release  deploy           user-invocable-only  static    297    74

skill_mode not honored on every configured harness (see docs/roles.md#skill_mode-on-other-harnesses):
  backend/review-pr = name-only: not applied on copilot, cursor; the skill stays listed there
```

`deploy-staging` is excluded by the parent role. `ai-rulez generate --role release-manager` writes the two skills
and sets their modes for each tool. Claude Code gets them as `skillOverrides` in `.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "skillOverrides": {
    "deploy": "user-invocable-only",
    "review-pr": "name-only"
  }
}
```

Cursor and Copilot read the shared `.agents/skills/`, where `user-invocable-only` becomes a frontmatter key:

```markdown
<!-- .agents/skills/deploy/SKILL.md -->
---
name: deploy
description: "Use when deploying to production."
disable-model-invocation: true
---
```

`name-only` has no equivalent there, so `review-pr` stays fully listed and `generate` warns.

#### Profiles vs roles

Both select a slice of the same content, but they answer different questions.

|              | Profile                            | Role                                       |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Question     | what does this repository ship?    | what does this person's job need?          |
| Scope        | the project or team                | a person (identity decided elsewhere)      |
| Selected by  | `--profile`, `default`             | `--role`                                   |
| Extra knobs  | none                               | per-kind selectors, `skill_mode`, `delivery`, `match`, `pin` |
| Compared by  | `tokens --compare-profiles`        | `tokens --by-role`                         |

Use a [profile](domains.md) when one checkout emits several project variants (a backend service, a frontend app) and
that choice belongs in the repository. Use a role when the same content is tailored to different people at
generation time. Domains are the shared vocabulary: profiles group domains for a project, roles group domains for a
person. Many projects keep a `default` profile for the repository and add roles for per-person variants.

#### Defining roles

Roles are a `[[roles]]` array in `config.toml`. Manifest settings live in a separate `[role_manifest]` table, because
TOML cannot use `roles` as both an array and a table.

| Key                                               | Type   | Meaning                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                                            | string | Lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`; unique. What `--role` takes.                                     |
| `description`                                     | string | Shown by `roles list`.                                                                                    |
| `domains`                                         | list   | Domains the role selects, as in a profile (`builtin:<name>` works too). Root content, globally enabled builtins and include-sourced domains are always kept. |
| `skills`, `rules`, `agents`, `commands`, `checks` | table  | `include` and `exclude` lists of item ids or [`path.Match`](https://pkg.go.dev/path#Match) globs. An entry with `/` matches `domain/id`. An empty `include` keeps everything the domains provide; `exclude` always wins. Context has no selector: context files always stay. |
| `skill_mode`                                      | table  | Skill id or glob to `on`, `name-only`, `user-invocable-only` or `off`.                                    |
| `delivery`                                        | table  | Skill id or glob to `static`, `served` or `both`; see [Delivery](#delivery).                              |
| `extends`                                         | string | One parent role.                                                                                          |
| `match`                                           | table  | `groups`: hint strings for an external tool. Not inherited.                                              |
| `pin`                                             | bool   | Record the digest of the role's rendered outputs in `ai-rulez.lock`. Not inherited.                       |

| `[role_manifest]` key | Default | Meaning                                                                              |
| --------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `enabled`             | `false` | write `.ai-rulez/roles.json` on `generate`; see [The roles manifest](#the-roles-manifest) |
| `skill_mode_fallback` | `drop`  | what `off` does where a tool cannot hide a skill; see [`skill_mode` on other harnesses](#skill_mode-on-other-harnesses) |

Roles can be overlaid in `config.local.toml` like profiles: entries merge by `name`, and `remove = true` drops a
shared role on your machine.

!!! warning "A role is a content filter, not an access boundary"
    A role narrows the rules, skills, agents, commands and checks that are rendered or served, and sets skill modes.
    It does not narrow hooks, `[permissions]`, `[[mcp_servers]]` or context files: those are rendered for every role.
    Do not use a role to withhold a tool or a credential; the outputs are plain files the holder can read and edit.

##### `skill_mode` precedence

For one skill, every matching key competes: an exact id beats a glob, a longer glob beats a shorter one, and a tie
goes to the lexically first pattern. A skill no key matches keeps the default, `on`.

Claude Code's `skillOverrides` is keyed by skill id, so two kept skills with the same id in different domains share
one entry. When the role gives them different modes, `validate` reports `AR971`; give both the same mode (a bare id
key does) or exclude one.

##### Inheritance

`extends` is one level deep: a role whose parent extends another role is an error. The child is merged over the
parent:

| Field                    | Merge                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `domains`                | union, parent first                                   |
| `exclude` lists          | union                                                 |
| `include` lists          | union when both set one, otherwise whichever is set   |
| `skill_mode`, `delivery` | merged; the child wins per key                        |
| `description`            | the child's, else the parent's                        |
| `match`, `pin`           | not inherited                                         |

##### Delivery

`[roles.delivery]` decides per skill whether the role's agent gets it as a file in the tool's skill folder (`static`),
only on demand from the [skills server](mcp-server.md#dynamic-skill-loading) (`served`), or both. Keys follow the
`skill_mode` rules, and entries are inherited with the child winning.

```toml
[[roles]]
name = "backend"
domains = ["backend"]

[roles.delivery]
"deploy-*" = "served"          # not listed in the agent's context; found with find_skill
"backend/runbooks" = "both"
```

For one skill, the first that is set wins: its own `delivery` frontmatter, the role, `[domains.<name>] delivery`,
`[skills] delivery`, then `static`. Everything that renders or serves a role uses it:

- `generate --role backend` leaves served skills out of the skill folders and adds the `dynamic-skills` skill;
- `tokens --role backend` does not count served skills in the listing and names them;
- `ai-rulez mcp --serve-skills --role backend` serves them, with `find_skill` scoped to the role;
- `roles resolve`, `roles.json` and `catalog` report each skill's delivery;
- `ai-rulez lock` pins the served skills of every role, so `[lock] enforce` covers them.

#### Commands

```bash
ai-rulez roles list [--format json]           # every role with item counts and token estimates
ai-rulez roles show <name> [--format json]    # as declared, and with the parent merged in
ai-rulez roles resolve <name> [--format json] # the items the role keeps, with sizes, modes and delivery

ai-rulez generate --role engineer             # project outputs for the role
ai-rulez generate --user --role engineer      # user-level outputs (~/.claude, ~/.codex, ...)
ai-rulez generate --check --role engineer     # drift check against the role's outputs

ai-rulez tokens --role engineer               # token surface of the role
ai-rulez tokens --by-role                     # one comparison column per role
```

- `--role` replaces profile selection and cannot be combined with `--profile` or `--plugin`. Everything in the run
  (outputs, token report, usage index) sees the role's slice.
- Installed skills scoped to profiles are not filtered by a role, and the machine-local `local/` tree is not
  narrowed.
- `generate --role` prints the role's `AR971` findings as warnings before it writes anything, so a typo in a domain or
  an `exclude` entry is visible.

#### Composing roles

`--role` takes a comma-separated list, as do `roles show`, `roles resolve`, `tokens --role` and
`mcp --serve-skills --role`. A composition is the union of its members: the domains and items they keep are combined,
and that union is rendered, served and counted.

```bash
ai-rulez generate --role engineer,oncall
ai-rulez roles resolve engineer,oncall
```

Where two members set `skill_mode` or `delivery` for the same skill, the [precedence](#skill_mode-precedence) applies
first (the more specific key wins); between equally specific keys, the role listed last wins. So `engineer,oncall`
and `oncall,engineer` can differ.

A composition is a value, not a `[[roles]]` entry: it cannot be extended, need not be declared, and every member must
exist (`AR971` otherwise). It can be pinned: `ai-rulez lock --role engineer,oncall` records the union's outputs under
the name `engineer,oncall`, and `generate --locked --role engineer,oncall` compares them. Pinning a member does not
pin the compositions that contain it, and the reverse.

#### `skill_mode` becomes Claude Code `skillOverrides`

| Mode                  | Claude Code behavior                                         |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `on`                  | listed with its description (the default)                   |
| `name-only`           | listed by name only, saving description tokens               |
| `user-invocable-only` | hidden from the model; you can still run it as `/name`      |
| `off`                 | hidden from the model and from you                           |

For every kept skill with a mode, `generate` writes `skillOverrides.<skill>` in `.claude/settings.json` (or
`~/.claude/settings.json` with `--user`) with the same per-key ownership as
[`[claude.settings.managed]`](settings.md):

- Only the skill ids the role lists are owned; other entries are left alone, and `clean` removes exactly what was
  written. A role's modes win over the same skill in `[claude.settings.managed] skill_overrides`.
- If you had set a different value for one of those ids by hand, `generate --role` warns, replaces it, and keeps
  yours in `<config dir>/local/.role-skill-overrides.json` (machine-local, gitignored). A plain `generate`, or a role
  that no longer lists the skill, restores your value.
- A value you change after the role wrote it is yours and is left alone.
- Switching roles removes the first role's entries and writes the second's. `mcp --serve-skills --role` never writes
  the settings file.

#### `skill_mode` on other harnesses

Only Claude Code has a per-skill settings key. For other tools, ai-rulez writes the mode into the skill's `SKILL.md`
frontmatter (or Codex's `agents/openai.yaml`) where the vendor documents an equivalent. A key you set in the skill's
own frontmatter is never overwritten.

| Preset          | `user-invocable-only`                                            | `off`                                                         | `name-only` |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `claude`        | `skillOverrides`                                                 | `skillOverrides`                                              | `skillOverrides` |
| `cursor`        | `disable-model-invocation: true`                                 | no documented setting                                         | no          |
| `codex`         | `agents/openai.yaml` `policy.allow_implicit_invocation: false`   | not rendered (Codex needs an absolute path)                   | no          |
| `copilot`       | `disable-model-invocation: true`                                 | `disable-model-invocation: true` and `user-invocable: false`  | no          |
| `opencode`      | no                                                               | not rendered (`permission.skill` in `opencode.json`)          | no          |
| `gemini`        | no                                                               | no settings key (only the `/skills disable` command)          | no          |
| other presets   | not documented                                                   | not documented                                                | not documented |

Where a cell says "no" or "not documented", the skill stays listed on that tool. `roles resolve` and `doctor` list
every skill and tool where a mode is not honored, and `generate` warns.

`off` hides a skill only when every configured tool can hide it. Otherwise `generate --role` follows
`skill_mode_fallback`:

```toml
[role_manifest]
skill_mode_fallback = "drop"   # drop (default) | serve
```

`drop` leaves the skill out of the role's render for every tool of the run, Claude Code included. `serve` switches it
to [served delivery](#delivery), so tools that can call MCP find it with `find_skill`.

#### Strict validation

| Code                                                    | Meaning                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`AR971`](strict-validation.md) `role-reference-unknown` | A domain that does not exist, or a selector, `skill_mode` or `delivery` entry that matches no item (or only items in a domain the role does not select). |
| [`AR972`](strict-validation.md) `role-extends-invalid`   | Unknown parent, cycle, or inheritance deeper than one level. Such a role is left out of `roles.json`.                           |
| [`AR973`](strict-validation.md) `role-unreachable-dependency` | An item the role keeps names, in its `skills:` frontmatter, a skill the role drops or hides with `off` or `user-invocable-only`. |

A bad name, a duplicate name or an invalid `skill_mode` or `delivery` value fails loading outright.

#### The roles manifest

With `[role_manifest] enabled = true`, `generate` writes `.ai-rulez/roles.json`; `roles list --format json` prints the
same document. It has no timestamps and is sorted (roles by name, items by kind, domain and id), so it is safe to
commit. It is built from the shared sources only: roles from `config.local.toml` and items under `local/` never
appear in it, so the file is the same on every machine. The schema is
[`schema/roles-manifest.schema.json`](https://github.com/Goldziher/ai-rulez/blob/main/schema/roles-manifest.schema.json).

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "tokenizer": "cl100k_base",
  "roles": [
    {
      "name": "engineer",
      "description": "Everyone who writes code",
      "match": { "groups": ["okta:eng"] },
      "domains": ["backend"],
      "skill_modes": { "review-pr": "name-only" },
      "items": [
        { "kind": "rule", "id": "commit-messages", "path": "rules/commit-messages.md", "bytes": 153, "tokens": 42 },
        ...
      ],
      "totals": {
        "items": 3, "bytes": 598, "tokens": 163, "by_kind": { "rule": 2, "skill": 1 },
        "served_skills": 0, "served_tokens": 0
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field                            | Meaning                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `items[].bytes`                  | size of the item's source files on disk (a skill counts its resources)                        |
| `items[].tokens`                 | estimate for the primary file (`SKILL.md`, the rule file), like every `ai-rulez tokens` figure |
| `items[].mode`, `items[].delivery` | the skill's resolved mode and delivery                                                       |
| `items[].owner`, `items[].version` | from the item's frontmatter, when set                                                        |
| `delivery`                       | the role's `[roles.delivery]` table                                                           |
| `totals.served_skills`, `totals.served_tokens` | skills that are served only, which cost no listing tokens until loaded             |

#### Integrating an identity tool or UI

Everything an integration needs is in versioned `--format json` output. ai-rulez never calls the network, and an
integration never parses config files.

1. **Discover the roles.** Read the committed `roles.json`, or run `ai-rulez roles list --format json`. Each role has
   its `name`, `description` and `match.groups`.
2. **Map a person to a role.** This is your tool's job: for example, read the person's identity-provider groups and
   pick the role whose `match.groups` contains one of them, by your own precedence when several match.
3. **Preview.** `ai-rulez roles resolve <name> --format json` lists the items the role keeps, with owner, version,
   bytes and tokens. `ai-rulez tokens --role <name> --format json` reports the token surface.
4. **Apply.** Run `ai-rulez generate --user --role <name> --yes` (user level) or `ai-rulez generate --role <name>`
   (project level). Exit code 0 means the files were written.
5. **Show the catalog.** `ai-rulez catalog --format json` lists every item with owner, version, size, digest, the
   roles that keep it and the lock status. See [Catalog](catalog.md) and
   [`schema/catalog.v1.schema.json`](https://github.com/Goldziher/ai-rulez/blob/main/schema/catalog.v1.schema.json).
6. **Audit.** [`ai-rulez lock --diff --format json`](lockfile.md) reports what changed between the committed lock and
   the working tree.

Every JSON document carries `schema_version`; refuse a version you do not know.

#### Roles and the lock file

The [lock file](lockfile.md) pins each role declaration (`kind = "role"`), so adding a role or changing what it
includes shows up in `lock --diff` and fails `lock --check`. A role's rendered outputs are pinned, as one digest per
role, when the role sets `pin = true` or with `lock --roles`. `lock --check --role <name>` and
`generate --check --locked --role <name>` then catch a change in what the role renders even when the sources are the
same (a new `skill_mode` entry, a new ai-rulez release); see [Composing with roles](lockfile.md#composing-with-roles).
Without a pin, `generate --locked --role <name>` still verifies that the sources match the lock. Served skills are
pinned as `[[served]]` entries; see [Served skills and skill sources](lockfile.md#served-skills-and-skill-sources).

## Includes

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/includes/

An include pulls rules, context, skills, agents, commands and checks from another directory or git repository into
your project, so an organization's standards are written once and shared by many repositories. Included content is
merged with your own before `generate` renders it, and your own content wins on a name collision.

#### Example

```toml
# .ai-rulez/config.toml
version = "5.0"
name = "web"
presets = ["claude", "cursor", "codex"]

[[includes]]
name = "standards"
source = "https://github.com/acme/ai-standards"
ref = "v1.2.0"
include = ["rules", "skills"]
```

The repository holds plain content folders, no configuration needed:

```text
ai-standards/
├── rules/
│   └── security.md
└── skills/
    └── security-review/
        └── SKILL.md
```

```markdown
<!-- ai-standards/rules/security.md -->
---
priority: critical
---

Never hardcode secrets. Validate all user input.
```

```bash
ai-rulez lock       # pin v1.2.0 to its commit
ai-rulez generate
```

The included rule lands in the shared `AGENTS.md` like one of your own:

```markdown
<!-- AGENTS.md -->
# web

## Rules

### security

**Priority:** critical

Never hardcode secrets. Validate all user input.
```

and the skill is written to `.claude/skills/security-review/` and `.agents/skills/security-review/` (Cursor and
Codex). If you add your own `.ai-rulez/rules/security.md`, it replaces the included one.

#### Include options

| Key                  | Type   | Default            | Meaning                                                                                       |
| -------------------- | ------ | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`               | string | required           | identifies the include in the lock, the cache and messages                                    |
| `source`             | string | required           | a git URL or a local directory; see [Sources](#sources)                                       |
| `path`               | string | source root        | subdirectory of the source to read (`modules/core`); a missing path fails the load            |
| `ref`                | string | the default branch | git branch, tag or commit                                                                     |
| `version`            | string | none               | git only: a semver range (`^1.2`, `~2.1.0`) resolved against tags, instead of `ref`; see [Version constraints](lockfile.md#version-constraints) |
| `tag_prefix`         | string | none               | with `version`: the tag prefix to match (`v`, `rules-`)                                       |
| `include_prerelease` | bool   | `false`            | with `version`: allow prerelease tags                                                         |
| `min_release_age`    | string | none               | with `version`: skip tags younger than this (`"7d"`)                                          |
| `include`            | list   | every kind         | kinds to import: `rules`, `context`, `skills`, `agents`, `commands`, `checks`                 |
| `install_to`         | string | root               | import the content into this domain instead of the root                                       |
| `merge_strategy`     | string | `local-override`   | who wins a name collision; see [Precedence](#precedence)                                      |
| `local_override`     | string | none               | a local directory used instead of `source`, for developing the include; see below             |
| `format`             | string | ai-rulez layout    | `okf` reads the source as an [OKF bundle](okf.md#okf-bundles-as-includes)                     |

- `include` filters content kinds, not domains: domains of an include are always carried over.
- MCP servers, hooks and other configuration are not imported, and an include's own `includes` are ignored. To
  combine several layers, list each one in your project.
- `local_override` is resolved against the project directory, with `path` appended. If the directory does not exist,
  the include is skipped with an info line; the remote source is not used instead. Because it bypasses the lock, it is
  honored only from `config.local.toml` or when no lock is enforced: `generate --locked`, `--frozen` and an enforced
  lock fail on a `local_override` in the committed config.

`ai-rulez include add|list|remove` edits the list:

```bash
ai-rulez include add standards https://github.com/acme/ai-standards --ref v1.2.0 --include rules,skills
ai-rulez include add mine ../my-rules --local      # into config.local.toml, for your machine only
ai-rulez include list
```

`--local` (and `local: true` on the MCP tool `add_include`) writes the include to `config.local.toml`. Overlay
entries merge with the shared list by `name`, and `remove = true` hides a shared include on your machine; see
[Local configuration](local-overrides.md).

#### Sources

| Form                | Example                                                             |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| HTTPS git           | `https://github.com/acme/ai-standards.git` (`.git` optional)        |
| SSH git             | `git@github.com:acme/ai-standards.git`, `ssh://git@host/acme/repo.git` |
| `git+` prefix       | `git+https://host/acme/repo` (same include and cache as without it) |
| local git repository| `file:///srv/git/ai-standards`                                      |
| local directory     | `./shared/standards`, `vendor/rules`                                |

Plain `http://` and `git://` remotes are rejected. SSH URLs use your git and SSH agent setup, which works for private
and self-hosted servers.

!!! warning "Local paths must stay inside the project"
    A local `source`, `path` or `local_override` in the project's committed config must resolve inside the project,
    symlinks included; otherwise loading stops with an error naming the path. This stops a repository from pulling
    `../victim` or `~/.config` into its generated files. For a directory elsewhere on your machine, declare the include
    in `config.local.toml` (`include add --local`) or in your user config (`generate --user`). The same holds for a
    `file://` URL; set `AI_RULEZ_ALLOW_FILE_URLS=1` in your environment to allow one in a project config.

##### Repository structure support

An include source can be laid out two ways, and ai-rulez detects which:

1. **Bare**: the directory has `rules/`, `context/`, `skills/`, `agents/`, `commands/` or `checks/` directly, at the
   root or under `path`. This is the simplest layout for a shared module.

   ```text
   shared-modules/
   └── modules/
       └── core/
           ├── rules/
           └── skills/
   ```

   ```toml
   [[includes]]
   name = "core"
   source = "https://github.com/acme/shared-modules.git"
   path = "modules/core"
   ```

2. **Wrapped**: the content is in a `.ai-rulez/` folder, as in a project that uses ai-rulez itself.

ai-rulez looks for a `.ai-rulez/` folder first (at the source root or under `path`), then for the bare folders.

`ai-rulez include add` with a local path accepts only the wrapped layout. Add a bare local directory by editing
`config.toml`.

#### Precedence

Your own content always wins. Includes are folded in the order they are declared, each with its own
`merge_strategy`:

| `merge_strategy`           | On a name collision with what is already merged             |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `local-override` (default) | the existing content wins: your project, then earlier includes |
| `include-override`         | this include wins, also over your project content           |
| `error`                    | `generate` fails, naming the include                        |

```toml
[[includes]]
name = "org"
source = "https://github.com/acme/org-rules"      # wins over "team" by default

[[includes]]
name = "team"
source = "https://github.com/acme/team-rules"
merge_strategy = "include-override"               # wins over "org" and over your own files
```

An item that collides across layers (for example a root rule from one include and a domain rule from an
`install_to` include) is collapsed by [name deduplication](configuration.md#deduplication-by-name): root wins over
domains, and `generate` warns with both paths:

```text
WARN  Duplicate rule collapsed name=security kept=shared/standards/rules/security.md dropped=shared/team/rules/security.md
```

#### Private repositories

Over SSH, your SSH keys and agent are used. Over HTTPS, set a token:

```bash
export AI_RULEZ_GIT_TOKEN="ghp_..."     # or pass --token on the command line
ai-rulez generate
```
